lines.text: How long does a bullet take?
lines.phonemes: hˌaʊ lˈɔŋ dˈʌz ɐ bˈʊlɪt tˈeɪk?

lines.text: A famous old photograph by Harold Edgerton shows a bullet going through an apple. That bullet flew at about eight hundred fifty meters a second. The apple is about eight centimeters across. So the bullet crosses it in less than a ten-thousandth of a second. Here, that takes about one second. The bullet is a small, dark shape. At this speed, you can watch it drift into the apple like a slow fish. The skin dimples. Then the back of the apple blows outward, in a spray. Pieces of the apple trail behind it, one at a time. And the bullet is already past. In real time, that was far too quick to blink. It's moving more than twice as fast as sound, so it drags a narrow cone of air behind it. Quick pause: if that one got you, tap like and follow. Okay, back to it. Even now, a table a meter wide would take it about twelve seconds to cross. A bullet is fast. But out the window, something is about to be much faster.
